questions.stem: The coefficient of the fourth term in the expansion of \((3x-4)^6\) is:
questions.hint: Fourth term means k = 3 in C(6,k)(3x)^(6−k)(−4)^k.

steps.explain: The general term is \(\binom{6}{k}(3x)^{6-k}(-4)^k\). The fourth term has \(k=3\) (the first term has \(k=0\)).
Compute the coefficient.
Watch the sign: \((-4)^3\) is negative. Using \(k=4\) (the fifth term) gives 25920.

keyPoints.note: The 4th term uses k = 3 (counting from k = 0). Keep the sign of (−4)³.

questions.stem: In how many different queues can 5 boys and 3 girls stand if the 3 girls must stand next to one another?
questions.hint: Treat the three girls as one block first, then arrange the girls within that block.

keyPoints.text: the 3 girls must stand next to one another
keyPoints.note: Group the girls as one block before counting the arrangements.

steps.explain: Treat the three girls as one block. The five boys and this block make six objects to arrange.
The three girls can change order within their block in 3! ways.
Multiply the independent choices to count every valid queue exactly once.

questions.stem: Each of the letters A, A, C, H, M, and S is written on a separate card. The cards are drawn at random from a hat and placed next to each other to form a word. What is the probability that the word ASCHAM appears?
questions.hint: Arrangements of letters with a repeat: divide by the factorial of the repeat.

steps.explain: Count the different arrangements of the 6 letters. The two A's are identical, so divide by \(2!\).
Exactly one of these arrangements spells ASCHAM.
Forgetting the repeated A gives \(\frac{1}{720}\).

keyPoints.text: A, A, C, H, M, and S
keyPoints.note: Two A's are identical, so the number of different words is 6!/2!.

questions.stem: 5 boys and 5 girls are seated at a round table. In how many ways can this happen with Robert and Hannah sitting together?
questions.hint: Treat the pair as one unit, use (n − 1)! for a circle, then ×2 for the pair's order.

steps.explain: Glue Robert and Hannah together as one unit. Then there are 9 units around the table.
Arrangements of \(n\) objects in a circle: \((n-1)!\).
Robert and Hannah can swap places within their unit.

keyPoints.note: Glue them into one unit (9 units round the table) and multiply by 2! for their order.

questions.stem: Given that \(n\) students are to be placed into 4 classrooms, what is the minimum number of students to guarantee that there are at least two students born in the same month in each of the 4 classrooms?
questions.hint: Pigeonhole: 13 students guarantee a shared month in one room; you need that in all 4 rooms.

steps.explain: Think of the worst case. A classroom can hold 12 students all born in different months without any repeat.
steps.work: \(12\ \text{months}\Rightarrow\text{up to }12\text{ students with no shared month}\)

steps.explain: To force a shared month, a classroom needs 13 students (pigeonhole principle: 13 students, 12 months).
Every one of the 4 classrooms must have this, and in the worst case the students are spread so each room has as few as possible. So we need 13 in each room.
With 51 students one room could have only 12 (all different months), so 52 is the minimum.

keyPoints.note: Each classroom needs 12 + 1 = 13 students to force a repeated month.

questions.stem: In how many ways can the letters of the word EXTENSION be arranged if the letter E’s are to be together?
questions.hint: Treat EE as one block (8 objects) and divide by 2! for the repeated N.

steps.explain: EXTENSION has 9 letters: E, X, T, E, N, S, I, O, N — two E's and two N's.
Glue the two E's into one block 'EE'. Now arrange 8 objects: (EE), X, T, N, S, I, O, N.
Divide by \(2!\) for the two identical N's. The E's inside the block are identical, so swapping them gives nothing new — no extra factor.
Option D. Dividing by another \(2!\) for the E's double-counts (they are already one block).

keyPoints.text: the letter E’s are to be together
keyPoints.note: Glue EE into one block; the only repeat left is the two N's.

questions.stem: Suppose there are \(n\) different books, and there are \(p\) identical copies of each of these \(n\) books. (You may assume \(n\) and \(p\) are non-zero integers by definition.)

parts.stem: If all the books are to be placed in a line on one shelf, in how many ways can this be done?
parts.hint: Arrangements with repeats: total! ÷ (repeat!) for each group.

steps.explain: There are \(np\) books in total. If they were all different there would be \((np)!\) arrangements.
Each title has \(p\) identical copies; swapping those copies changes nothing, so divide by \(p!\) for each of the \(n\) titles.

keyPoints.text: in how many ways can this be done
keyPoints.note: np books in total; divide by p! for each of the n groups of identical copies.

parts.stem:
Consider now a library with \(n\) different books, where there are \(p\) identical copies of each of these \(n\) books on one shelf. The library barcodes each book differently to keep track of each book in its catalogue.

Suppose you want to borrow at least one book from the shelf, but you do not want to borrow multiple copies of the same book (despite the different barcodes). In how many ways can this be done?

(To clarify: At the borrowing desk, the librarian will scan out copy 1 of Book A differently to copy 2 of Book A because they have different barcodes.)
parts.hint: Each title: one of p copies or none (p + 1 choices). Then remove the 'borrow nothing' case.

steps.explain: For each of the \(n\) titles, decide what to do: take copy 1, copy 2, …, copy \(p\) (different barcodes), or take none of that title.
The choices for different titles are independent, so multiply.
This includes the one case where no book is taken at all. You must borrow at least one, so subtract it.

keyPoints.note: For each title there are p + 1 choices (a specific copy or none); subtract the empty choice.

questions.stem: Nine points are given, with exactly four lying on one straight line and no other three collinear. How many triangles can be formed using the points as vertices?
questions.hint: Count all triples of points, then remove triples chosen entirely from the four collinear points.

keyPoints.note: A triple from those four points does not make a triangle.

keyPoints.text: four lying on one straight line
keyPoints.note: Only the all-collinear triples need to be removed.

steps.explain: Choose any 3 of the 9 points.
Remove the triples selected from the four collinear points; these do not form triangles.
Subtract the invalid triples.
